paper.title: MELD: Recursive Self-Improvement via Hierarchical Coordination for Multi-Agent Scientific Discovery
paper.abstract: Multi-agent scientific discovery with large language models raises a coupled learning problem: research assignments determine both which experiments are pursued and the experiences from which agents adapt. We introduce MELD, a unified hierarchical test-time training framework that jointly adapts a team-level Coordinator policy and agent-level individual Scientist policies within a single discovery process. The Coordinator generates a joint portfolio of search branches and research directives over a shared derivation tree, while Scientists develop hypotheses and execution plans implemented by a shared frozen Executor. Both levels receive alternating GRPO-style parameter updates under a shared smooth best-of-budget objective, allowing team organization and individual research behavior to co-evolve in a recursive self-improvement loop. Our analysis establishes objective alignment for the hierarchy, characterizes conditions for coordination gains over independent parallel discovery and the first-order benefit of private adaptation, and derives a finite-budget regret bound for adapted models. On 22 MLGym and MLE-bench tasks, MELD is best on 20 of them and achieves the highest aggregate normalized scores on MLGym, using a 4B backbone for coordination and research. Most baselines use proprietary Scientists, and all systems share one frozen Executor.

research_problem.text: 研究分配同时影响团队进展与后续学习经历。作者将单次发现过程中联合学习团队协调和个体研究策略定位为现有方法尚未解决的问题；该前作判断未独立核验。

evidence.quote: For a team of collaborative agents, each local research assignment determines both the team’s overall progress and the learning experience that shapes the team’s subsequent research strategy.

These advances leave a central joint learning problem unresolved: how can a team-level coordination policy and individual agent-level research policies be learned together within a single discovery process?

method_steps.text: 用共享派生树及剩余预算表示发现状态。Coordinator一次生成联合分配，从至多16个节点中选择父节点并指定研究问题、瓶颈与约束；各Scientist生成假设和执行计划。

evidence.quote: At round t , the shared history is represented by a rooted derivation tree \mathcal{G}_{t}=(V_{t},E_{t}) , whose root stores (c_{0},s_{0}) . Together with the remaining budget b_{t} , it defines the discovery state \mathcal{S}_{t}=(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{G}_{t},b_{t}) .

The Coordinator emits the complete portfolio in one schema-constrained JSON completion of at most 1200 tokens containing, for each unit, a parent identifier chosen from a retrieved shortlist of at most 16 tree nodes (at most two nodes from the same family) and a free-text directive with three fields (research question, observed bottleneck, constraints).
Each Scientist emits a hypothesis and an execution plan of at most 3400 tokens for its assignment.

In a Coordinator group , each fork samples a complete portfolio Z^{(g)}\sim\pi^{\mathrm{coord}}_{\phi_{\mathrm{old}}}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{S}) and executes its units using the current Scientist policies. In a Scientist group , one portfolio Z is fixed across forks,

author_contributions.text: 作者自述提出层级测试时训练框架，在一个未见任务内联合适配两层策略，并由更新后的策略生成后续学习经历，形成递归自改进闭环；创新优先性未独立确认。

evidence.quote: We introduced Meld , a hierarchical TTT framework that jointly adapts team-level Coordinator and agent-level Scientist policies on one unseen task. Updated policies generate the experience and feedback for later adaptation, forming a recursive self-improvement loop with team-level coordination and agent-level research exploration.

author_contributions.text: 作者自述建立层级目标对齐分析，研究匹配边际分布与预算下的条件性协调收益、共同初始模型处私有适配的一阶收益，并推导有限预算遗憾界和条件性优化速率。

evidence.quote: Our theoretical analysis establishes objective alignment for the proposed hierarchy, characterizes conditions for coordination gains over independent parallel discovery at matched individual outcome distributions and budgets, and quantifies the first-order benefit of private adaptation at a common model.
We further derive a finite-budget regret bound for adapted models and a conditional optimization rate.

Multi-agent scientific discovery with large language models raises a coupled learning problem: research assignments determine both which experiments are pursued and the experiences from which agents adapt.

The Coordinator generates a joint portfolio of search branches and research directives over a shared derivation tree, while Scientists develop hypotheses and execution plans implemented by a shared frozen Executor.
These system-level comparisons use a 4B backbone for Meld ’s coordination and research, proprietary Scientist models for most baselines, and the same frozen Executor throughout.
For a team of collaborative agents, each local research assignment determines both the team’s overall progress and the learning experience that shapes the team’s subsequent research strategy.

These advances leave a central joint learning problem unresolved: how can a team-level coordination policy and individual agent-level research policies be learned together within a single discovery process?

At round t , the shared history is represented by a rooted derivation tree \mathcal{G}_{t}=(V_{t},E_{t}) , whose root stores (c_{0},s_{0}) . Together with the remaining budget b_{t} , it defines the discovery state \mathcal{S}_{t}=(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{G}_{t},b_{t}) .

Each Scientist emits a hypothesis and an execution plan of at most 3400 tokens for its assignment.

We introduced Meld , a hierarchical TTT framework that jointly adapts team-level Coordinator and agent-level Scientist policies on one unseen task. Updated policies generate the experience and feedback for later adaptation, forming a recursive self-improvement loop with team-level coordination and agent-level research exploration.

Our theoretical analysis establishes objective alignment for the proposed hierarchy, characterizes conditions for coordination gains over independent parallel discovery at matched individual outcome distributions and budgets, and quantifies the first-order benefit of private adaptation at a common model.
We further derive a finite-budget regret bound for adapted models and a conditional optimization rate.
